                     MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF
                               ENCHANTED ROCK, LLC

         Pursuant to Rules 212 and 2131 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”

or “Commission”)’s rules of practice and procedure, Enchanted Rock, LLC (“ERock”2) submits

this motion for leave to answer (“Motion”) and answer (“Answer”) in response to PJM

Interconnection, LLC (“PJM”)’s April 24, 2026 reply brief3 in the captioned proceedings

concerning, inter alia, the Commission’s December 18 Order.4

         ERock submits this Answer to respond to several misleading and incorrect statements

made by PJM in their April 24 Reply Brief concerning PJM’s proposed implementation of

Interim Network Integration Transmission Service (“Interim NITS” 5). Moreover, for the

PJM’s proposed implementation of Interim NITS conflicts with the December 18 Order’s

directives requiring PJM to establish “a new interim, non-firm transmission service.”7

I.      MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

        While Rule 213(a)(3) of the Commission’s rules of practice and procedure provides that

an “answer may be made to any pleading, if not prohibited under paragraph (a)(2) of this

section,”8 Rule 213(a)(2) precludes, as a matter of right, an answer to a protest or answer.9 The

Commission, however, will permit such answers for good cause shown.10 Good cause exists

when the response will assist the Commission in its decision-making process, such as by helping

to explain the relevant issues or otherwise facilitating the development of the record.11 Good

cause exists here to allow ERock to respond to the April 24 Reply Brief in order to address

several erroneous arguments made by PJM, and to facilitate the development of the record.

II.     ANSWER

        A.       PJM’s Proposed Implementation of Interim NITS Is Fundamentally Flawed

        At the heart of PJM’s proposed implementation of Interim NITS lies a fundamental

disconnect between what PJM is proposing and what the Commission directed PJM to

implement in the December 18 Order. Notably, after finding that PJM’s existing tariff is unjust

and unreasonable because, inter alia, “it does not include transmission services that reflect an

 Eligible Customer taking service on behalf of a Co-Located Load that is willing and able to limit

its energy withdrawals from the transmission system under certain conditions,”12 the

Commission directed PJM to “establish three new transmission services that reflect that Eligible

Customers taking service on behalf of Co-Located Load are willing and able to limit their energy

withdrawals from the transmission system under certain conditions.”13 Relevant here, one of the

three new types of transmission services is intended to “allow Eligible Customers seeking to take

NITS on behalf of Co-Located Load to, at their option, take a new interim, non-firm

transmission service until all Network Upgrades necessary to provide NITS are complete.”14

        Rather than proposing rules that would enable Eligible Customers to utilize this “new

interim, non-firm transmission service,” the April 24 Reply Brief instead doubles down on PJM’s

flawed position that would prohibit Co-Located Load from receiving any capacity or energy

from a Co-Located Generating Facility while the Co-Located Load is taking Interim NITS

(sometimes referred to herein as the “Proposed Interim NITS Limitation”).15 PJM’s Proposed

Interim NITS Limitation, and its statements in its April 24 Reply Brief, make clear that PJM

seeks to treat a Co-Located Generating Facility serving a Co-Located Load taking Interim NITS

as a Capacity Resource that is fully deliverable to the PJM wholesale market during the interim

period before “all Network Upgrades necessary to provide NITS are complete”16 and before the

Co-Located Generating Facility even has an executed Generator Interconnection Agreement

(“GIA”). PJM’s Proposed Interim NITS Limitation thus directly frustrates the Commission’s

intention to allow a load taking interim, non-firm transmission service, and that is co-located

 with a generator, to be served by such generator before both the load and generator “‘graduate’ to

full, front-of-meter service.”17

        For these reasons, and the reasons discussed further herein and in the ERock Protest,

PJM’s proposed implementation of Interim NITS clearly runs afoul of the Commission’s

applicable directives in the December 18 Order and should be rejected by the Commission.

        B.      Responses to Specific PJM Statements and Arguments in the April 24 Reply Brief

        The fundamental disconnect between PJM’s proposed implementation of Interim NITS

and the Commission’s applicable directives manifests in several of PJM’s statements and

positions set forth in its April 24 Reply Brief, as addressed below.

        First, PJM recognizes that the December 18 Order held that “when curtailed, Eligible

Customers taking [Interim NITS] on behalf of Co-Located Loads may be able to continue to take

energy from the Interconnection Customer with which they are co-located if PJM’s Tariff

otherwise allows.”18 Rather than explaining why its tariff would not otherwise allow a Co-

Located Load to take energy from a Co-Located Generating Facility (i.e., the Interconnection

Customer), or even proposing new tariff language that would codify such prohibition, PJM

instead states that it “thoroughly examined whether the Tariff should allow Interim NITS

customers to directly take energy from the Co-Located Generating Facility when PJM has

curtailed the Eligible Customer’s access to the Transmission System” and determined that it

should not.19

        PJM’s Proposed Interim NITS Limitation thus clearly departs from the Commission’s

directive because PJM has not identified any tariff provisions that would not “otherwise allow” a

 Co-Located Load from receiving any capacity or energy from a Co-Located Generating Facility

while the Co-Located Load is taking Interim NITS. Moreover, for the reasons explained by

ERock in its Protest, PJM’s Proposed Interim NITS Limitation would need to be codified in the

PJM Tariff (PJM’s filed rate) in order to be effectuated because it is a practice, inter alia, “that

affect[s] rates and service significantly, that [is] reasonably susceptible of specification, and that

[is] not so generally understood in any contractual arrangement as to render recitation

superfluous.”20 Accordingly, for these reasons alone, the Commission should reject PJM’s

Proposed Interim NITS Limitation.

         Second, PJM avers that its Proposed Interim NITS Limitation is in line with the

December 18 Order’s requirement that Interim NITS be designed around the principles that “(1)

the services are designed to serve loads that are ‘willing and able to control their withdrawals

from the transmission system;’ and (2) the services are designed to allow PJM to maintain

system reliability,”21 and that “Interim NITS will be curtailed when the system cannot support it

in real time, whether with sufficient generation or transmission capacity.”22 But PJM’s argument

misses the mark entirely, as the ability for a Co-Located Load to take energy and capacity from a

Co-Located Generating Facility during the interim period before “all Network Upgrades

necessary to provide NITS are complete,”23 enables the Co-Located Load “to control their

 withdrawals from the transmission system.”24 Further, as made clear in Commissioner Rosner’s

concurrence in the December 18 Order, the Commission knew that large load customers taking

Interim NITS would only be “willing and able to control their withdrawals from the transmission

system,” if they could rely upon their Co-Located Generating Facility during the interim period

before necessary Network Upgrades are constructed.25 PJM’s Proposed Interim NITS Limitation

thus directly contradicts the Commission’s directive for PJM to establish an interim, non-firm

transmission service.

         Third, PJM appears to believe that requiring the Co-Located Generating Facility to be

fully deliverable as a Capacity Resource during the interim period is necessary to “allow PJM to

maintain system reliability.”26 PJM avers that allowing a Co-Located Generating Facility to

serve a Co-Located Load utilizing Interim NITS would “remove the co-located generator from

serving the Transmission System as a whole during emergency or pre-emergency conditions,”27

and states that “to the extent the co-located generator is a committed Capacity Resource, the PJM

Region has first call on such resource’s energy to meet the region’s needs.”28 But PJM’s

argument is inherently flawed because prior to the Co-Located Generating Facility completing

PJM’s interconnection study process and receiving a GIA, it is not eligible to be a Capacity

Resource.

         ERock does not object to limiting a Co-Located Load from receiving any capacity or

energy from a Co-Located Generating Facility during emergency conditions once the Co-

Located Generating Facility has gone through the interconnection study process, has received a

GIA, is a Capacity Resource, and the Co-Located Load receives firm service following the

completion of necessary Network Upgrades.29 However, imposing such restrictions during the

interim period prior to the Co-Located Generating Facility receiving a GIA, and prior to such

Network Upgrades being completed, would not allow PJM to in fact call on the Co-Located

Generating Facility as a Capacity Resource to meet any emergency. Further, such restrictions

would render Interim NITS unworkable and conflict with the Commission’s directives regarding

Interim NITS.30

        Moreover, during the period in which the Co-Located Load operates on a non-firm basis,

PJM can curtail the Co-Located Load during emergencies in order to maintain the reliability of

the overall system, while the Co-Located Generating Facility can serve the Co-Located Load so

that it does not go entirely offline. This arrangement enables PJM to maintain the overall

reliability of the system while encouraging large loads to be curtailable by allowing them to rely

on their Co-Located Generating Facility until both the load and generating facility “graduate” to

full, front of meter service, as the Commission intended.31 This is not what PJM proposed.

Further, forcing the Co-Located Generating Facility to be dispatched under emergency

conditions during the interim period before it has completed the generation interconnection study

process, has a GIA and is eligible to be a Capacity Resource, would not only conflict with the

Generating Facilities because it would impose obligations upon them that are not imposed upon

similarly situated generators in PJM, i.e., generators that are in the process of being studied to be

Capacity Resources but are not Co-Located Generating Facilities.32

         Lastly, PJM argues that it would be illogical to allow Interim NITS customers to rely on

their non-firm Co-Located Generating Facilities during emergencies when full NITS customers

cannot. PJM goes so far as to argue that it is “illogical to grant this right to the transitional,

temporary Interim NITS when such right is not available to full NITS customers.”33 But PJM

has it backwards. Instead, it would be illogical for the Interim NITS customer not to be allowed

to rely on its non-firm Co-located Generating Facility in order to remain online during

emergencies when it is taking non-firm transmission service precisely because it is not taking

firm transmission service under NITS.34

         Further, it would be illogical (and not just and reasonable) to have a Co-Located Load

taking Interim NITS bear the full capital and development risk of bringing a Co-Located

Generating Facility online, only for PJM to dispatch their non-firm Co-Located Generating

Facility for the benefit of other customers with firm NITS during emergencies – which is

precisely when other customers with firm NITS are being served, but the non-firm, Interim NITS

customer is being curtailed. PJM’s proposal would thus create an inequitable, unjust and

 unreasonable situation where firm NITS customers would receive emergency reliability benefits

at the direct expense of Interim NITS customers.

III.       CONCLUSION

           PJM should not be allowed to openly flout the Commission’s unequivocal directives in

the December 18 Order. The Commission required PJM to establish “a new interim, non-firm

transmission service,”35 that will allow a load that is co-located with a generator to “take service

directly from the generator in the interim until both ‘graduate’ to full, front-of-meter service” so

that the load will not “always have to shut down completely during peak periods.”36 Rather than

complying with these and related directives, PJM’s Proposed Interim NITS Limitation undercuts

them. Accordingly, for the reasons set forth herein, ERock respectfully requests that the

Commission grant its Motion, consider this Answer and prohibit PJM from imposing its

Proposed Interim NITS Limitation.
